full_text_en:
Zhengzhou Municipal People's Procuratorate v. Huang Xin — intentional homicide

Procuratorial Authority: People's Procuratorate of Zhengzhou City, Henan Province.

Defendant: Huang Xin, male, 31 years old, company employee, residing at Dongming Road, Zhengzhou City, Henan Province. Placed under residential surveillance on October 26, 1998, and arrested on November 3 of the same year.

The case of Defendant Huang Xin for intentional homicide was initiated by the People's Procuratorate of Zhengzhou City, Henan Province, by way of public prosecution before the Zhengzhou Intermediate People's Court, Henan Province, on February 1, 2001.

Indictment Allegations: On the evening of October 23, 1998, Defendant Huang Xin and his girlfriend Liu Yan were playing cards at the home of Wang Sanmei, a fellow villager of Liu Yan. During the card game, an argument occurred between Huang and Liu, after which the two returned together to their cohabitation residence. Around 9:00 a.m. the next morning, Huang Xin left the residence. At approximately 10:30 a.m., Liu Yan's father, Liu Zhuanyun, went upstairs to check the telephone line and discovered that Liu Yan had been killed. Forensic examination determined: Liu Yan died from mechanical asphyxia combined with hemorrhagic shock caused by strangulation of the neck and a stab wound to the left neck inflicted by a single-edged sharp instrument. The time of death was approximately around 1:00 a.m. on October 24, 1998. Based on on-site investigation and interrogation of Huang Xin, as well as the forensic determination of Liu Yan's time of death, the public security authorities established that only Huang Xin was present at the time Liu Yan was killed. Relying on Huang Xin's confession, witness testimony from Liu Zhuanyun and others, expert conclusions, on-site inspection records, and relevant verification results, the prosecutorial authority alleged that Huang Xin intentionally and unlawfully deprived Liu Yan of her life, causing her death, and that his conduct constituted the crime of intentional homicide.

Defendant Huang Xin denied killing Liu Yan.

Defendant Huang Xin's defense counsel argued: The prosecutorial authority's allegation that Defendant Huang Xin committed intentional homicide, based solely on the expert conclusion regarding Liu Yan's time of death, seriously fails to meet the statutory standard of proof requiring that evidence be "reliable and sufficient." In this case, Huang Xin had no criminal motive to intentionally kill Liu Yan; the time of Liu Yan's death as determined in the indictment is clearly inconsistent with the postmortem phenomena described in the criminal technical examination report, including livor mortis, cornea, and pupils; and the detection of "a large amount of sperm" in the victim's body that did not belong to Huang Xin indicates that Liu Yan may have been killed by another person after Huang Xin left. The case of Liu Yan's death should be reclassified and investigated as a rape-homicide case.

During the court investigation, the prosecution and defense conducted cross-examination of the evidence submitted by the prosecutorial authority:

1. All statements provided by the prosecutorial authority from Defendant Huang Xin, witness testimony from Liu Zhuanyun, Ren Sumian, Wang Sanmei, and others, as well as Huang Xin's in-court statements, can prove: On the evening before the incident, Huang Xin and Liu Yan had an argument while playing cards at Wang Sanmei's home. On the day of the incident, at approximately 9:00 a.m., Huang Xin left Liu Yan's home and had a conversation with Liu Yan's mother, Ren Sumian. After leaving Liu Yan, Huang Xin went to help his sister purchase computer components. At around 10:30 a.m., Liu Zhuanyun discovered that his daughter Liu Yan had been killed.

Defendant Huang Xin argued that he did not kill Liu Yan, stating that from the evening of the 23rd until approximately 9:00 a.m. the next day, he and Liu Yan were together the entire time, and that Liu Yan was still alive when he left. Defense counsel argued: The fact that Huang Xin and Liu Yan had an argument cannot prove that Huang Xin had a motive to kill Liu Yan.

2. The on-site inspection record in the "Scene" section of the Criminal Technical Examination Report No. (98) Gong Fa Yi Jian Zi No. 243 (hereinafter "Report No. 243") submitted by the prosecutorial authority, concerning the scene of Liu Yan's murder, states: The scene of Liu Yan's death was located on the west side of the second floor, in a one-bedroom, one-living-room apartment. The door lock was intact, with no signs of forced entry; the toilet window was open, the screen window was closed, with no signs of climbing; the west and south bedroom windows were aluminum alloy sliding windows, with no signs of climbing.

Defendant Huang Xin's defense counsel argued: The relevant description in the "Scene" section of the criminal technical examination report is incorrect. Photographs of the crime scene show that the aluminum alloy sliding window and screen window on the west side of the bedroom were both open, while the aluminum alloy sliding window on the south side of the bedroom was open and the screen window closed.

3. Report No. 243 submitted by the prosecutorial authority states: "Based on the autopsy findings, scattered patchy abrasions and subcutaneous hemorrhages were present on the front and right side of the victim's neck. A horizontal, closed-loop ligature mark was found at the level of the thyroid cartilage. Subcutaneous and muscle tissue hemorrhage in the neck, combined with signs of asphyxia such as cyanosis and swelling of the face, punctate hemorrhages in the conjunctiva, and punctate hemorrhages under the epicardium and pulmonary pleura, indicate that Liu Yan was manually strangled (by hand) and ligature-strangled (by electrical cord) before death, causing mechanical asphyxia. A dagger was inserted into the victim's neck. Examination revealed that the wound track ran obliquely downward and inward, causing a through-and-through wound of the left internal jugular vein and transection of a branch of the left subclavian artery, with massive accumulation of blood in the left thoracic cavity. Combined with pale livor mortis and pallor of both lungs — signs of blood loss — this indicates that Liu Yan was stabbed in the left neck with a single-edged sharp instrument (dagger) while her heart had not yet completely stopped, causing massive blood loss." "Liu Yan died from mechanical asphyxia combined with hemorrhagic shock caused by strangulation of the neck and a stab wound to the left neck inflicted by a single-edged sharp instrument."

Defendant Huang Xin's defense counsel argued: The source of one of the murder weapons, the dagger, is unknown, and no fingerprints were recovered from the weapon. There is no evidence proving that Huang Xin manually strangled, ligature-strangled with an electrical cord, or stabbed Liu Yan in the left neck with a single-edged sharp instrument, thereby causing her death.

4. Report No. 243 submitted by the prosecutorial authority, Physical Evidence Examination Report No. (9*) Gong Wu Zheng Jian Zi No. 3994 from the Ministry of Public Security, Expert Conclusion No. (2000) Gao Jian Ji Jian No. 05 from the Supreme People's Procuratorate (hereinafter "Conclusion No. 05"), and research records concerning Liu Yan's time of death prepared by forensic experts from provincial and municipal authorities, all indicate that Liu Yan's time of death was approximately 1:00 a.m. or 2:00 a.m. on October 24, 1998.

Defendant Huang Xin's defense counsel argued: There are doubts regarding the conclusion on Liu Yan's time of death. First, the conclusion on Liu Yan's time of death was based solely on the phenomenon of algor mortis, without considering important factors that affect algor mortis and thus the estimation of time of death, such as the fact that the victim was naked, had suffered massive blood loss, and was lying on a non-wooden floor. Second, Report No. 243 records that the victim's "livor mortis was distributed over the unpressured areas of the back, pale purplish-red, partially fading with finger pressure," "cornea transparent," "pupils round and dilated, approximately 0.5 cm in diameter." According to forensic medical literature, these postmortem phenomena should appear within 2-3 hours, within 1 hour, and within 4 hours after death, respectively. These postmortem phenomena of the victim are inconsistent with a death occurring 12 hours earlier, indicating that the forensic conclusion estimating the victim's death at 12 hours prior is unreliable. Third, the Physical Evidence Examination Report No. (99) Gong Wu Zheng Jian Zi No. 3904 from the Ministry of Public Security does not bear the signature of the examiner and should not be used as evidence for deciding the case; the meeting minutes of relevant departments studying Liu Yan's time of death do not fall within the categories of evidence specified in the Criminal Procedure Law and lack evidentiary effect; Conclusion No. 05 from the Supreme People's Procuratorate was made based on Report No. 243 from the Zhengzhou Public Security Bureau and has limited evidentiary value.

5. Physical Evidence Inspection Report No. (98) Gong Wu Zheng Jian Zi No. 3059 from the Ministry of Public Security, submitted by the prosecutorial authority, states: "A large amount of sperm was detected in the vaginal swab of Liu Yan, and A and B blood group substances were detected." Physical Evidence Examination Reports No. (98) Gong Wu Zheng Jian Zi No. 3276 and No. (2001) Gong Wu Zheng Jian Zi No. 2303 from the Ministry of Public Security confirmed that "the DNA genotype of this sperm differs from the DNA genotype of Huang Xin."

Defense counsel argued: The presence of a "large amount of sperm" from another person in the victim's body indicates that the time of Liu Yan's death should have occurred after Huang Xin left Liu Yan at approximately 9:00 a.m. on the 24th. Based on the fact that all three examination reports from the Ministry of Public Security describe the "brief case facts" as "Liu Yan was raped and killed," this case should be classified as a rape-homicide case.

The Zhengzhou Intermediate People's Court holds:

For a prosecutorial authority to charge a defendant with a crime, it must ensure that the facts alleged are clear and the evidence is reliable and sufficient. In this case, based on the existing evidence, the facts concerning the motive alleged in the indictment — that Defendant Huang Xin killed Liu Yan — are unclear and the evidence is insufficient. According to the evidence, the means used by the perpetrator to kill Liu Yan included manual strangulation, ligature strangulation with an electrical cord, and stabbing the left neck with a single-edged sharp instrument, causing Liu Yan to die from "mechanical asphyxia combined with hemorrhagic shock." However, the evidence presented by the prosecutorial authority cannot prove that Huang Xin committed this direct and specific act that killed Liu Yan. The only evidence supporting the indictment that Huang Xin committed intentional homicide is the sole indirect evidence of the expert conclusion regarding Liu Yan's time of death. Yet, the postmortem phenomena of the victim recorded in the criminal technical examination report — such as livor mortis, cornea, and pupils — when used to estimate the time of death according to forensic medical literature, show an obvious contradiction with the expert conclusion on Liu Yan's time of death, and the existing evidence cannot reasonably explain this contradiction. During the court investigation, the prosecutorial authority failed to provide explanations for significant doubtful issues, such as "from whom did the large amount of sperm in the vaginal secretions of the deceased Liu Yan originate" and "whether Liu Yan was raped by another person before her death," and the existing evidence cannot reasonably explain these issues either. This indicates that the facts of this case have not been clarified, and the existing evidence provided by the prosecutorial authority is clearly insufficient to prove that Liu Yan was killed by Huang Xin. Because the facts are unclear and the evidence is insufficient, the charge by the People's Procuratorate of Zhengzhou City that Defendant Huang Xin killed Liu Yan cannot be established and is therefore not supported. The defense arguments and opinions of Defendant Huang Xin and his defense counsel — that the prosecutorial authority's allegations are based on unclear facts and insufficient evidence — are established in law and shall be adopted.

Accordingly, on July 30, 2002, the Zhengzhou Intermediate People's Court, pursuant to Article 162(3) of the Criminal Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, rendered the following judgment:

Defendant Huang Xin is not guilty.

This judgment has become legally effective.
